structured_output.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, woody plants (trees) have unisexual (separate male and female) flowers at a higher rate than herbaceous plants, and this holds across plant orders/families rather than only in a few lineages.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Using species with known sexual system and growth form, the proportion with separate sexes (dioecious + monoecious, i.e. unisexual flowers) is higher in woody than herbaceous species, with a pooled difference of at least 5 percentage points (Fisher/chi-square p<0.01), AND among families containing at least 20 species of each growth form, at least 60% show a higher woody proportion (one-sided binomial test vs 50%, p<0.05). The same direction in the dioecy-only proportion is required as a secondary check.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The pooled woody-minus-herbaceous difference in proportion of unisexual-flowered species is below 5 percentage points or reversed, OR fewer than 55% of qualifying families show a higher woody proportion, OR the dioecy-only proportion is not higher in woody species.
structured_output.interpretation: Darwin's 'trees belonging to all Orders' is mapped to species coded 'woody' in the dataset (trees, shrubs, woody lianas). This is broader than trees alone, so it is a modern reinterpretation, and trees cannot be separated from shrubs in the summary categories. 'Other plants' maps to herbaceous (herbs, herbaceous lianas, subshrubs). 'Sexes separated' maps to dioecy (separate male and female individuals, including gynodioecy/androdioecy/polygamodioecy) plus monoecy (separate male and female flowers on the same plant). The claim names 'separate male and female flowers', so monoecy plus dioecy is primary and dioecy alone is secondary. Orders are approximated by families, which the dataset records. Hooker's Australian exception is not tested, since the dataset is global and a regional test is out of scope. Darwin's data were British, and this dataset is global, so it tests the generalization 'across all orders' and not the British observation.

dataset.name: Global distribution and evolutionary transitions of angiosperm sexual systems
dataset.publisher: Dryad (Wang, Luo, Lyu, Dimitrov, Xu, Freckleton, et al.)
dataset.why_it_fits: The dataset records sexual system (dioecy, monoecy, hermaphroditism) and growth form (woody vs herbaceous) for about 67,000 angiosperm species across 355 families. It lists downloadable CSVs: SplistWithSexSyst.csv (species-level list with sexual system, growth form, family; field names are to be confirmed from the README xlsx) and GloSexSyst.csv. The fields used are family, growth form and sexual system. The dataset is global, so it tests the cross-order generalization, not the British sample.
